questions.question_text:
A watermelon is weighed as $5.84$ kg.
What is the precision of this measurement?

options.why: Took the first decimal place as the smallest place value instead of the hundredths.
Found the absolute error, which is half the precision, instead of the precision itself.
Used the whole-number place value, ignoring the decimal places of the reading.

questions.solution_text:
The smallest place value of $5.84$ kg is the hundredths.
$\text{Precision} = 0.01$ kg

options.why: Gave the precision — the size of one division — without halving it.
Assumed the divisions are $1$ cm apart instead of reading the $2$ cm spacing from the labels.
Took half the whole range shown on the diagram instead of half of one division.

questions.solution_text:
The smallest division on the tape is $2$ cm.
$\text{Precision} = 2$ cm
$\text{Absolute error} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2$
$= 1$ cm

questions.question_text:
A ribbon is measured as $9.3$ cm long.
What is the absolute error of this measurement?

options.why: Gave the precision without halving it to find the absolute error.
Treated the precision as $1$ cm, ignoring the decimal place, then halved it.
Halved the measurement itself instead of halving the precision.

questions.question_text:
A road is $570$ km long, to the nearest $10$ km.
What is the absolute error of this measurement?

options.why: Gave the stated precision of $10$ km without halving it.
Ignored the 'nearest $10$ km' and used a precision of $1$ km.
Halved the absolute error a second time, taking half of $5$ km.

questions.question_text: A muffin is weighed as $24$ g. What is the lower bound of its true mass?

options.why: Subtracted the whole precision of $1$ g instead of the absolute error of $0.5$ g.
Added the absolute error, giving the upper bound instead of the lower bound.
Used an absolute error of $0.05$ g, as if the measurement were given to one decimal place.

questions.question_text:
A reaction time is recorded as $6.8$ s, rounded to the nearest $0.1$ s. Halfway values round up.
Between which limits must the true time $t$, in seconds, lie?

options.why: Used an absolute error of $0.5$ s, treating the precision as $1$ s instead of $0.1$ s.
Added and subtracted the whole precision of $0.1$ s instead of half of it.
Used a precision of $0.01$ s, one place value smaller than the reading shows.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{Precision} = 0.1$ s
$\text{Absolute error} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.1$
$= 0.05$ s
$\text{Lower bound} = 6.8 - 0.05$
$= 6.75$ s
$\text{Upper bound} = 6.8 + 0.05$
$= 6.85$ s
The lower endpoint rounds to $6.8$ s; the upper endpoint rounds to $6.9$ s.
$6.75 \leq t < 6.85$

questions.question_text:
A dog is weighed as $65$ kg, to the nearest $5$ kg. Halfway values round up.
Between which limits must its true mass $m$, in kilograms, lie?

options.why: Ignored the 'nearest $5$ kg' and used a precision of $1$ kg.
Added and subtracted the whole precision of $5$ kg instead of half of it.
Halved the absolute error a second time, using $1.25$ kg instead of $2.5$ kg.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{Precision} = 5$ kg
$\text{Absolute error} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 5$
$= 2.5$ kg
$\text{Lower bound} = 65 - 2.5$
$= 62.5$ kg
$\text{Upper bound} = 65 + 2.5$
$= 67.5$ kg
The lower endpoint rounds to $65$ kg; the upper endpoint rounds to $70$ kg.
$62.5 \leq m < 67.5$

questions.question_text:
Ada, Ben and Cara each correctly measure the length of the same bench.
Ada records $3.6$ m, Ben records $3.64$ m and Cara records $4$ m. How can all three measurements be correct?

options.text: They used measuring instruments with different precision.
Each measurement is exact, with no possible rounding error.
options.why: Treated rounded measurements as exact, although each has an absolute error equal to half its precision.

options.text: All three instruments have a precision of $1$ m.
options.why: Ignored the decimal places: Ada's possible precision is $0.1$ m and Ben's is $0.01$ m.

questions.solution_text:
Ada: precision $0.1$ m
Ben: precision $0.01$ m
Cara: precision $1$ m
They used instruments with different precision, so the same length can be rounded to different smallest units.
For example, a length of $3.642$ m rounds to $3.6$ m, $3.64$ m and $4$ m at these precisions.

questions.question_text:
The mass $m$ of a parcel, in kilograms, has the limits of accuracy $5.5 \leq m < 6.5$. Halfway values round up.
What is its mass correct to the nearest kilogram?

options.why: Rounded down from the lower endpoint, although $5.5$ kg rounds up to $6$ kg.
Read the lower bound as the rounded measurement instead of rounding to the nearest kilogram.
Read the excluded upper bound as the rounded measurement instead of rounding to the nearest kilogram.

questions.solution_text:
Every value from $5.5$ kg up to, but not including, $6.5$ kg rounds to $6$ kg.
The mass correct to the nearest kilogram is $6$ kg.
